title: Celsus’s own warning against demon worship
source_text: Ὑπιδόμενος γοῦν ὁ Κέλσος τὸν εἰς μαγείαν ὄλισθον τῶν τὰ τοιαῦτα μεμαθηκότων καὶ συναισθηθείς πως βλάβης περὶ τοὺς ἀκούοντας ἐσομένης φησίν· ἐκεῖνο μέντοι φυλακτέον, ὅπως μή τις συνὼν τούτοις τῇ θεραπείᾳ τῇ περὶ αὐτὰ συντακῇ, φιλοσωματήσας τε καὶ τῶν κρειττόνων ἀποστραφεὶς λήθῃ κατασχεθῇ. χρὴ γὰρ ἴσως οὐκ ἀπιστεῖν ἀνδράσι σοφοῖς. οἳ δή φασι διότι τῶν μὲν περιγείων δαιμόνων τὸ πλεῖστον γενέσει συντετηκὸς καὶ προσηλωμένον αἵματι καὶ κνίσσῃ καὶ μελῳδίαις καὶ ἄλλοις τισὶ τοιούτοις προσδεδεμένον κρεῖττον οὐδὲν δύναιτ᾿ ἂν τοῦ θεραπεῦσαι σῶμα καὶ μέλλουσαν τύχην ἀνθρώπῳ καὶ πόλει προειπεῖν, καὶ ὅσα περὶ τὰς θνητὰς πράξεις ταῦτα ἴσασί τε καὶ δύνανται. τηλικούτου οὖν ὀλίσθου περὶ τὸν τόπον ὄντος, ὡς καὶ ὁ ἐχθρὸς τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀληθείᾳ μαρτυρεῖ. πόσῳ βέλτιον χωρὶς πάσης ὑφοράσεως ὑπὲρ τοῦ συντακῆναι τοιούτοις δαίμοσιν ἢ φιλοσωματῆσαι καὶ τὰ κρείττονα ἀποστραφῆναι καὶ ὑπὸ λήθης τῆς τῶν κρειττόνων κατασχεθῆναι τὸ ἑαυτὸν ἐμπιστεῦσαι τῷ ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεῷ διὰ τοῦ τὴν τοιαύτην ἡμῖν διδασκαλίαν ὑποθεμένου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ καὶ ἀπ᾿ ἐκείνου αἰτεῖν πᾶσαν βοήθειαν καὶ φρουρὰν τὴν ἀπὸ ἁγίων ἀγγέλων καὶ δικαίων, ἵν᾿ ἡμᾶς ῥύσωνται ἀπὸ τῶν περιγείων δαιμόνων καὶ γενέσει συντετηκότων καὶ αἵματι καὶ κνίσσῃ προσηλωμένων καὶ ἀλλοκότοις μελῳδίαις ἀγομένων καὶ ἄλλοις τοιούτοις προσδεδεμένων, ὁμολογουμένως μὲν καὶ κατὰ τὸν Κέλσον κρεῖττον οὐδὲν δυναμένων τοῦ θεραπεῦσαι τὸ σῶμα. ἐγὼ δ᾿ εἴποιμ᾿ ἂν ὅτι οὐδ᾿ ἐναργές ἐστι τὸ τοὺς δαίμονας τούτους ὅπως ποτὲ θεραπευομένους δύνασθαι θεραπεύειν τὰ σώματα· ἀλλὰ χρὴ τὴν θεραπείαν τῶν σωμάτων, εἰ μὲν ἁπλούστερον βούλοιτό τις ζῆν καὶ κοινότερον, ἐφόδῳ ἰατρικῇ θεραπεύειν, εἰ δὲ βέλτιον παρὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς. εὐσεβείᾳ τῇ εἰς τὸν ἐπὶ πᾶσι θεὸν καὶ ταῖς πρὸς ἐκεῖνον εὐχαῖς.
pass_a_gloss: Celsus, having suspected (ὑφοράω) the slide (ὄλισθος) into magic (μαγεία) of those who have learned such things, and having somehow perceived (συναισθάνομαι) harm (βλάβη) that would be for the hearers, says: this must be guarded against (φυλακτέον), that no one, consorting (σύνειμι) with these, melt away (συντήκομαι) into the service (θεραπεία) about them, and having come to love the body (φιλοσωματέω) and turned away (ἀποστρέφομαι) from the better things (τὰ κρείττονα), be held fast (κατέχω) by forgetfulness (λήθη). For perhaps one must not disbelieve (ἀπιστέω) wise men (ἄνδρες σοφοί), who say that the greater part of the earthly demons (περίγειοι δαίμονες), melted into generation (γένεσις) and nailed (προσηλόω) to blood (αἷμα) and savour of sacrifice (κνῖσα) and melodies (μελῳδίαι) and bound (προσδέω) to other such things, could do nothing better than to heal a body and foretell (προλέγω) coming fortune (τύχη) to a man and a city, and whatever concerns mortal actions (θνηταὶ πράξεις), these things they know and can do. There being so great a slide about the subject (τόπος), as even the enemy (ἐχθρός) bears witness (μαρτυρέω) to the truth (ἀλήθεια) of God, how much better, without all suspicion (ὑφόρασις) of melting into such demons, or loving the body and turning from the better things and being held by forgetfulness of the better things, to entrust (ἐμπιστεύω) oneself to the God over all through Jesus Christ, who laid down (ὑποτίθημι) such teaching (διδασκαλία) for us, and to ask from Him all help (βοήθεια) and guard (φρουρά) from holy angels (ἅγιοι ἄγγελοι) and righteous (δίκαιοι), that they may rescue (ῥύομαι) us from the earthly demons melted into generation and nailed to blood and savour and led (ἄγω) by strange (ἀλλόκοτοι) melodies and bound to other such things, admittedly (ὁμολογουμένως) even according to Celsus able to do nothing better than to heal the body. I would say that it is not even evident (ἐναργές) that these demons, served (θεραπεύω) however, can heal (θεραπεύω) bodies; but one must see to the healing of bodies, if one wishes to live more simply (ἁπλούστερον) and more commonly (κοινότερον), by medical method (ἔφοδος ἰατρική), but if better than the many, by piety (εὐσέβεια) toward the God over all and prayers (εὐχαί) to Him.
pass_b_english: Celsus, at any rate, suspected that those who have learned such things slide into magic, and he somehow sensed that harm would come to those who heard them. So he says: “One must, however, guard against this: that no one, by keeping company with these beings, should be wholly absorbed in their worship, and, coming to love the body and turning away from higher things, be held fast by forgetfulness. For perhaps we ought not to disbelieve wise men, who say that most of the earthly demons are fused with the world of becoming, nailed to blood and the smoke of sacrifice and to songs, and bound to other such things, and could do nothing better than heal a body and foretell the coming fortune of a man and of a city; and all that concerns mortal affairs, this they know and can do.”

Since the danger of slipping in this matter is so great, as even the enemy bears witness to the truth of God, how much better it is, free from any fear of being absorbed into such demons, or of loving the body, turning away from higher things and being held fast by forgetfulness of higher things, to entrust oneself to the God over all through Jesus Christ, who gave us such teaching, and to ask from Him all help and the protection of holy angels and of the righteous, so that they may rescue us from the earthly demons. These are fused with the world of becoming, nailed to blood and the smoke of sacrifice, drawn by outlandish songs and bound to other such things, and, as even Celsus admits, can do nothing better than heal the body.

But I would say that it is not even clear that these demons, however they are served, can heal bodies. Rather, if a person wishes to live in a simpler and more ordinary way, he should see to the healing of the body by medical means; but if he wishes to live better than the many, by piety toward the God over all and by prayers to Him.

choices.choice: Celsus’s words run from ‘One must, however, guard’ to ‘know and can do’; his phrases are then echoed by Origen without quotation marks because Origen reworks them. τῇ θεραπείᾳ τῇ περὶ αὐτά: αὐτά (neuter) is taken to refer to the demons (δαιμόνια, neuter, used by Origen in 8.58), hence ‘their worship’. συντακῇ / συντετηκός (‘melt into’) rendered ‘be wholly absorbed in’ and ‘fused with’. γένεσις rendered ‘the world of becoming’ (the realm of birth and change). κνῖσα rendered ‘the smoke of sacrifice’ (the savour of burnt fat). Origen plays on θεραπεύω, ‘serve’ and ‘heal’ (‘however they are served, can heal’), which the English keeps. ὁ ἐχθρὸς τῇ τοῦ θεοῦ ἀληθείᾳ μαρτυρεῖ: the dative goes with μαρτυρεῖ (‘even the enemy bears witness to the truth of God’); ‘the enemy’ is Celsus. Koetschau’s stops after μαρτυρεῖ and πολλούς are read as pauses inside the sentence. No Scripture is quoted. Review: the dative could also go with ἐχθρός (‘even the enemy of God’s truth bears witness’); both readings make Celsus testify against himself, and the draft’s reading is kept.
περὶ τοὺς ἀκούοντας: dropped added 'to him' ('those who heard them')
συνὼν τούτοις made instrumental ('by keeping company with these beings')
'every help and the guard' to 'all help and the protection' (βοήθειαν, φρουράν); ἀγομένων 'drawn'
ἐφόδῳ ἰατρικῇ 'by medical means'; elided βούλοιτο ζῆν made explicit in the last clause
